t: A systematic review of specialised word lists
Distinctive linguistic features in academic journal registers across disciplines: A key feature analysis
Characterizing Finnish children’s books by target age — Complementing key feature analysis with machine learning
abs: This study applies corpus linguistic and machine learning methods to analyze 300 Finnish children’s books intended to be read between the ages of 7 and 15, and examines the linguistic characteristics and distinctiveness of texts written for particular ages. The corpus we use, the Turku Children’s Book Lexicon (TCBC), consists of three sub-corpora based on the intended reading ages of the books ( 7-8 , 9-12 , 13-15 ) and we use two different methodologies to analyze the linguistic characteristics of texts in these age groups. First, we use Key Feature Analysis (Egbert and Biber 2023) to examine the typical functional features of texts on the corpus level. Second, for examining the distinctiveness of the text classes on the level of individual texts, we use interpretable machine learning methods and Support Vector Machines (SVM) in particular. In our analysis, we use a total of 148 features. We show that the texts in each age group have distinct linguistic characteristics, with differences in phrasal and clausal complexity, morpho-lexical richness, and lexical variation. However, classifying individual texts proves quite difficult and machine learning models struggle especially with distinguishing texts of the middle age group from the others. We also show empirical evidence that traditionally used readability metrics are insufficient for characterizing text classes. This study provides crucial information for a wide range of fields applying age-specific text data, such as psycholinguistic reading studies and the development of education technologies.

t: Measuring Vocabulary in Mechanical Engineering Textbooks across Subjects
abs: This article reports on a corpus-based study examining vocabulary of textbooks used as reading materials in twelve subjects under the domain of mechanical engineering at a higher education institution in the China context. The present study aims to exam the vocabulary demand of mechanical engineering textbooks and to create a Mechanical Engineering Word List to cover the EFL undergraduates’ lexical shortage. It first presents the vocabulary profiles of subject texts from the domain of mechanical engineering using Nation’s (2020) British National Corpus/Corpus of Contemporary American English (BNC/COCA) word frequency lists. Then, it outlines the vocabulary load required to comprehend different subjects of texts within twelve sub-corpora. The results indicate that students need to contain at least 4 th to 7 th BNC/COCA list word family to reach the 95% lexical comprehension, which is too much burden. The findings suggest that lexical demands vary when handling reading materials across different subjects in mechanical engineering, and provide insights into the extent of vocabulary knowledge needed to understand and learn different subject content through texts. After analysis of the lexical load of textbook texts across subjects, a Mechanical Engineering Word List (MEWL) is needed to help students acquire the 95% lexical coverage to reach the minimally adequate comprehension with less reading burden.

t: Lexical proficiency and automated proficiency detection: Assessing the utility of frequency, context, and semantics
Corpus sense 2: a re-engineered platform for corpus exploration and analysis
abs: Corpus Sense is a web application for content and discourse analysis designed to make advanced corpus exploration accessible to a broad range of user profiles, from corpus linguists to social scientists with no technical background. The original version, described in Moreno-Ortiz (2025), combined traditional corpus analysis methods with natural language processing and AI-assisted functionalities: keyword extraction, named entity recognition, semantic search, topic modelling with labels generated by a large language model (LLM), and LLM-generated insights. This paper presents version 2.0, a major release that re-engineers the platform and extends its analytical tool set. The monolithic implementation of the first version has been replaced by a modular platform with asynchronous background processing: analytics become available as soon as linguistic parsing completes, long-running analyses no longer tie the user to an open browser tab, and new tools can be added without structural rework. On this foundation, version 2.0 delivers the functionalities identified as priorities in the original paper: grammatical collocation analysis with an interactive navigator, n-gram extraction with C-value scoring and interactive curation, transformer-based sentiment and emotion classification with corpus trajectories, and metadata-based subcorpora, together with corpus-wide dispersion and evenness statistics and a redesigned WordMap visualisation. Every tool from the first version has been revised. The paper describes the new architecture, the revised and new tools, and the platform’s AI-assisted features; it situates the collocation and n-gram tools against Sketch Engine, AntConc, WordSmith Tools, CQPweb and LancsBox, including an empirical comparison, and closes with a roadmap of further modules.

t: Enhancing second language learning through corpus and GenAI integration: A systematic review
The Parallel Corpus of Chilean Literature: Compilation and Use
Environmental or economic crisis: A multi-method analysis of green energy transition in left- and right-leaning UK newspapers 2015-2024
Saudi Statutes in English Translation: A Corpus-Based Comparison With US Statutes for Localised Legal English Pedagogy
Moving beyond genre: Mapping student writing in a multidimensional situational space
abs: While research on academic writing has long recognised the importance of text types, consistent and principled classification has remained problematic. Existing taxonomies often prove difficult to apply to new corpora, and key terms (e.g., exposition, narrative) are inconsistently defined. Taxonomies have also been criticised for failing to capture the diversity and dynamism of academic writing and for encouraging formulaic teaching practices. Building on work by Biber, Egbert, and Keller (2020), this paper develops an alternative approach that may provide a more nuanced and dynamic representation by viewing text type variation as continuous and multidimensional, rather than categorical. We develop a detailed set of situational parameters to describe variation in student writing and apply them to a balanced sample of texts from the British Written Academic English (BAWE) corpus. Using factor analysis, we identify four key dimensions of variation: (1) explicit library research, (2) focus on quantitative data vs. individuals, (3) reporting a research or design process, and (4) personal informal writing. These dimensions are proposed as a flexible heuristic for understanding how student texts vary within and across traditional categories.By mapping corpus texts on our dimensions, we empirically characterize traditional genres as cultural constructs, highlighting their core features, overlaps, and disciplinary differences. We also show how individual texts can be positioned in relation to these dimensions and genres. We argue that this multidimensional approach offers a more coherent and adaptable framework for analysing variation in academic writing, with important implications for English for Academic Purposes (EAP) pedagogy and research.

t: The formula transition énergétique in a French-Language newspaper: toward a tool enhanced methodological framework for French-Language discourse analysis
Exploring the diagnostic potential of lexical bundles within departmental contexts: A focus on literature writing in an English department in Lebanon
“You’re not ‘choosing’ to fare evade, you’re just ‘trying to get to work’ so you can eventually have money.”: The discursive construction of transport precarity on Reddit
The dynamics of pragmatics and lexico-grammatical productivity in the Standard Marine Communication Phrases: A corpus-based exploratory study
abs: This article proposes additional SMCP-compatible phrases for harbour towage communication and demonstrates the productive potential of the IMO’s Standard Marine Communication Phrases (IMO, 2002) as a specialised controlled language through corpus-informed pragmatic analysis. A corpus-based comparison between the existing SMCP phrase inventory and a specialised corpus of harbour towage guidance docuements reveals a number of communicative gaps in exchanges involving the Tug Master and the Pilot or, depending on the operational context, the Master. Rather than departing from the principles on which the SMCP were conceived, the study formulates additional phrases that remain consistent with their grammatical, lexical, semantic, and functional constraints. To this end, the analysis combines two specialised English corpora: an SMCP corpus containing the existing towage- and pilotage-related phrases, and a purpose-built corpus of harbour towage guidelines used to identify communicative situations not currently covered. These data are examined through pragmatic annotation and lexico-grammatical pattern extraction in order to map communicative functions onto recurrent SMCP phrase structures and use them as templates for phrase generation. The results show that the proposed procedure makes it possible to formulate new phrases in a controlled and linguistically consistent way, thereby broadening SMCP coverage in the harbour towage domain, confirming the productive capacity of this specialised controlled language, and supporting further phrase development in other underrepresented areas of maritime communication.

t: Predicting difficulty of English derivations for L2 learners using usage-based metrics: A comparison to word frequency measures
abs: Usage-based models (Bybee, 2006; Tomasello, 2003) suggest that multiple derivations of a given headword cannot be considered equally difficult, because the frequency and distributions of their various affixes influence the likelihood that an L2 learner can determine their meaning. Author (2025) proposed usage-based metrics to describe derivations in relation to affix frequency, semantics, and form. Such metrics may improve frequency-based models of derivational difficulty. In this study, multiple regressions were run to predict difficulty of derived forms for 446 Japanese EFL learners using five such metrics: affix type frequency, affix type–token ratio, relative entropy, contingency, and proportion of known basewords, along with the more common predictors of derivational (lemma) and word family frequency. Lemma and word family frequency were found to make contributions unique to one another when explaining variance, and two usage-metrics (affix frequency and relative entropy) appeared to explain residuals to the word frequency-based predictors, and consequently were highly significant ( p < .001) in the final model, with a reciprocal suppression effect heightening their significance after frequency measures were added. An additional major finding was that, rather than being competing measures of word frequency that researchers must choose between, lemma and word-family frequency explain unique variance, and their concurrent use improves predictions of derivation difficulty.

t: Constructing newsworthiness in institutional research press releases: An applied corpus study
abs: This paper looks at the under-researched genre of the institutional research press release, examining how the writers of these press releases recontextualise scientific/academic research as news. To approach this, it first takes the concept of Discursive News Values (DNVs), and conducts a quantitative study of the way these are reflected in three different moves within the text: the headlines and leads, the body of the text, and the quotations from experts. The results confirm previous research that identifies a special role not only for the headline and lead, but also for the quoted material, and extends our knowledge by quantifying the presence of DNVs in each move and investigating the roles they play. This paper shows how the re-contextualisation of research as news is habitually accomplished through the effective operationalisation of DNVs in distinct ways in these three major areas of the text.

t: Methodological pathways to measuring visibility and attention
YouTA: A context-aware corpus annotation tool for critical discourse analysis of YouTube comments
abs: YouTA (YouTube Text Annotator) is presented as a context-aware corpus annotation tool that bridges Critical Discourse Analysis (CDA) theory and computational analysis by addressing limitations in existing annotation environments for Systemic Functional Linguistics (SFL)-informed research. The tool integrates four innovations: (i) context-aware annotation linking text to YouTube metadata; (ii) SFL-compatible hierarchical multi-label annotation; (iii) a human-augmented Large Language Model (LLM)-assisted workflow with provenance tracking; and (iv) an ISO-standardized interface design minimizing cognitive load. This architecture preserves situational and interactional context while supporting complex annotation schemes and enabling qualitatively informed quantification. To demonstrate its methodological contribution, a case study is included in which mental processes are annotated across a subset of YouTube comments using the human–LLM workflow. Results show that LLMs provide effective first-pass annotations (F1 = 0.578; partial-overlap recall = 0.693), with approximately 41% of annotations directly accepted, around 11% requiring boundary refinement, and the remainder either rejected or missed, reflecting a workflow in which the majority of relevant instances are either correctly identified or partially captured by the model. YouTA thus facilitates the systematic integration of linguistic theory, annotation practice, and scalable computational analysis, while maintaining human interpretive agency.

t: Distinguishing B1 and B2 writing: A multidimensional analysis of syntactic complexity in Vietnamese EFL learners
Corpus-informed AI-likeness screening for L2 writing: A proof-of-concept field test and two flagged cases
abs: Generative AI has expanded the range of support available for L2 writing, including idea generation, language revision, feedback, and grammatical assistance, but it has also intensified concern about outsourcing in unsupervised assignments. Existing AI detectors show uneven accuracy, vulnerability to circumvention, and fairness risks in multilingual settings. In response, this proof-of-concept field test examined AI-Likeness Inspector, a teacher-facing prototype that uses corpus-informed, interpretable linguistic indices for low-stakes screening. The prototype operationalizes indices and the fixed reference threshold from Mizumoto et al. (2024), including an errors-per-100-words threshold of 3.44, and applies them to task-matched L2 writing. Under the same essay prompt and task conditions as Mizumoto et al., 142 first-year university students submitted 200–300-word argumentative essays online. Two submissions (1.4%) fell below the fixed error-rate threshold and were treated as cases for follow-up rather than as proof of AI authorship. Follow-up interviews with both students indicated that each had used ChatGPT to draft the essay and had prompted the model to include deliberate errors to appear more human. The findings therefore support a narrow conclusion: transparent, task-specific screening can help identify atypical submissions for further checking, but this study does not estimate sensitivity, specificity, or false negative rates and should not be read as validation of a general-purpose detector.

t: What words matter most in legal English? A corpus-driven study of lexical coverage and the mid-frequency lexical core
Exploring the language of endometriosis: Between media representation and social construction
abs: This paper explores the language of endometriosis as used by different communities in French. Key actors of health communication in this context are included (women with endometriosis, healthcare professionals, patient associations, journalists). From a corpus-based perspective, the approach combines two methods aiming at identifying lexical differences, keyword analysis and term extraction, which yield results of different kinds. While keywords aim at examining the most salient lexical differences in each community compared to the others, terms aim at exploring terminological usage in the subcorpora through the units recognised as terms. The observation of selected keywords reveals the diversity of themes associated with endometriosis in the subcorpora, from diagnosis and research methods in specialised discourse to feminist and gender equality issues in the press. Terms are investigated through their distributional environments in the subcorpora. Syntactical differences in the use of verbs such as opérer [operate] highlight usage specific to women with endometriosis and reflect, to some extent, their experiential expertise. Shared collocations across all subcorpora (e.g. rapport sexuel douloureux [painful sexual intercourse]) reveal differences in function through their broader distributional contexts: some uses, specific to healthcare professionals, reflect objective ways of assessing sexual function, while others, specific to patient associations, aim at challenging established assumptions. Overall, this paper sheds light on the specificities of the discourses on endometriosis in French, while offering new insights into the processes of term circulation and appropriation and providing a solid basis for further exploring their implications for public knowledge and collective understanding of the condition.

t: Surprise words and core words: Collocational divergence across corpora
abs: This paper introduces a method for identifying words whose collocational behaviour differs across corpora. While keyword analysis identifies differences in relative frequency, it does not systematically identify words that are used in different contexts across corpora. To address this gap, this paper proposes the concept of collocationally divergent words, or surprise words (s-words), defined as words whose collocational profiles strongly differbetween two corpora. A related term - core words (c-words) are those which show high collocational similarity between two corpora. A list of divergence scores for all candidate words are calculated by comparing the similarities between the top collocates of each word across corpora. In order to implement this concept, this paper also describes the development of the S-Word Analysis Tool (SWAT), created using the Large Language Model ChatGPT. The tool automatically identifies and ranks words according to their collocational divergence and provides collocate lists and concordances to enable qualitative analyses to be carried out. A case study comparing representations of obesity in The Guardian and The Sun shows that s-words reveal differences in discourse framing not identified through keyword analysis alone, particularly in relation to responsibility, cost and solutions. The paper argues that s-word analysis provides a complementary method for corpus comparison and demonstrates the potential of large language models for developing new corpus linguistic tools and methods.

t: Can AI speak authentically: A multi-dimensional analysis of ChatGPT-generated dialogue and learner dialogue on a persuasion task
‘Women with chronic pain’: A diachronic corpus-assisted analysis of the gender pain gap in Australian news (2011–2025)
Ending in English: Collocation, semantic preference, prosody, and transitivity in ‘put an end to’, ‘bring an end to’, and ‘come to an end’
‘Not as a cure but as a way to prolong life’ – A diachronic corpus-assisted discourse analysis of the representations of immunotherapy in a UK-based online cancer forum
Communicating climate change in UK parliamentary politics: Discursive fluctuation over time
abs: This paper examines how UK politicians discuss climate change and how this evolves over time. Using the Hansard corpus for parliamentary debates in the UK House of Commons, we analyse the relative stability or changeability of collocates of “climate” during a ten-year period (2014–2023). The study takes a corpus-assisted discourse studies (CADS) approach, applying collocational Usage Fluctuation Analysis (UFA) to a corpus of approximately 100 million words in order to identify and track climate collocates according to their consistency or type of changeability (transient, initiating, or terminating). Findings reveal three periods or points of relative stability/consistency (2014–2017, 2021, 2023) and two periods of change (2018–2020, 2021–2022). Consistent collocates of “climate” variably refer to the economy or economic issues related to climate change, metaphors of war/conflict that highlight climate action and climate change impact, and what we identify as a form of climate exceptionalism or leadership. Notable patterns of change include the transitory inclusion of other voices (scientists, young people, activists). They also include the initiation of more varied and nuanced journey metaphors related to climate action, reference to climate change as a crisis or emergency, and more explicit discussion of nature and the natural environment. These patterns of fluctuation are interpreted in light of a variety of key social, political, and climactic events during the ten-year period, e.g. amendments to the UK Climate Change Act and the emergence and activities of new climate activist groups.

t: A Corpus-based comparative study of four-word lexical bundles in interpreted and non-interpreted English at UN Security Council meetings
Lexical blending and dehumanisation in misogynistic hate speech: A cognitive, corpus‑assisted study of foid
abs: • The blend foid shows ‑oid as the parameter shaping mechanistic dehumanisation. • Verb patterns reveal sexualised harm when foid is an object and low‑agency framing when it is a subject. • Modifiers reinforce dual dehumanisation, combining animalistic vilification with mechanistic objectification. • Fine‑grained analysis of foid + be highlights definitional environments tied to dehumanising attributes. • Granular corpus evidence supports a usage‑based definition distinguishing mechanistic and animalistic senses. NIncel discourse constitutes a form of online hate speech against women, mainly located in the digital manosphere and specific forums. It is characterised by extremist misogyny and recurrent self-victimisation, whereby incels frame themselves as powerless and dominated by women. This study examines the relationship between incel language and emotion by analysing dehumanization strategies through a cognitive corpus-assisted approach. The Incelcor corpus, consisting of 229 posts retrieved from incel forums, was compiled for this purpose. The analysis focuses on the blend foid ( female + android ). Corpus-assisted discourse analysis was combined with cognitive linguistics to examine the behaviour of the blend when it acts as subject/object and the interaction with its modifiers. Besides, cognitive modelling has been addressed in order to explore the granular dimension of the term under study. With the linguistic evidence and instances, a usage-based dictionary entry has been proposed distinguishing the two folded dehumanization strategies identified in the blend. Linguistic evidence reflects that incels made use of victimization in their speech, and their perpetration of linguistic and symbolic violence lies on these mechanisms of dehumanization and victimization. Granularity played a key role in the study of this salient term as it allowed to zoom on the lexical and discursive levels, also capturing elaboration through the study of collocational patterns. There are limitations that should be acknowledged like the corpus size, the specialized dataset and the absence of experimental measurements that empirically linked language and emotions.

t: The Litkey Corpus: How a longitudinal corpus of primary school children’s texts can be used for studying spelling and writing development in German
abs: We present research on the Litkey Corpus ( Laarmann-Quante et al., 2019c ), a longitudinal collection of German texts produced by primary school children between 2nd and 4th grade. With its multilevel annotations on the word level, including phonemes, syllables, morphemes, and error annotations, the corpus is particularly suitable for the study of orthography acquisition. This corpus-based approach complements experimental studies on spelling development, and offers a range of methodological approaches that come with their own strengths and weaknesses, as we will showcase in this contribution. Laarmann-Quante (2021) used machine learning methods to predict how likely words are to be misspelled and what (combination of) features make words particularly error-prone. In lemma-level analyses, the corpus has been used for studying vocabulary growth during the primary school years. In two pilot studies, we used a network science approach and explored various measures of lexical diversity to characterize how the lexical knowledge of children with different levels of orthographic proficiency develops ( Wieler, 2026 , Laâguidi et al., 2024 ). As a final example, we show how the Litkey Corpus can be used to study the development of syntactic complexity in the children’s texts, even in the absence of syntactic and morphosyntactic annotations ( Laâguidi et al., 2024 ). With each of the studies we review, we discuss important caveats that result from idiosyncrasies of working with corpus data. In closing, we discuss desirable extensions of the corpus that would allow it to be used to study morphosyntactic development.

t: Increasing translation accuracy for grammaticalized bei2 in Cantonese: A corpus-linguistic approach to machine translation disambiguation
A corpus-based investigation on approximations Shàngxià and zuǒyòu in Mandarin
A multifactorial analysis of the acquisition of Chinese causative constructions by CSL learners: A corpus-based study of shi and rang
A comparative study of rhetorical moves and linguistic features of DeepSeek-R1-generated and human-written academic chinese abstracts in empirical research
Metaphor identification using large language models: A comparison of RAG, prompt engineering, and fine-tuning
abs: Metaphor is a pervasive feature of discourse and a powerful lens for examining cognition, emotion, and ideology. Large-scale analysis, however, has been constrained by the need for manual annotation due to the context-sensitive nature of metaphor. This study investigates the potential of large language models (LLMs) to automate metaphor identification in full texts. We compare three methods: (i) retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), where the model is provided with a codebook and instructed to annotate texts based on its rules and examples; (ii) prompt engineering, where we design task-specific verbal instructions; and (iii) fine-tuning, where the model is trained on hand-coded texts to optimize performance. Within prompt engineering, we test zero-shot, few-shot, and chain-of-thought strategies. Our results show that state-of-the-art closed-source LLMs can achieve high accuracy, with fine-tuning yielding a median F1 score of 0.79. A comparison of human and LLM outputs reveals that most discrepancies are systematic, reflecting well-known grey areas and conceptual challenges in metaphor theory. We propose that LLMs can be used to at least partly automate metaphor identification and can serve as a testbed for developing and refining metaphor identification protocols and the theory that underpins them.

t: The written production in learner French (WIF) corpus: a new resource for examining children’s writing
abs: This article accounts for research on Swedish children’s writing in French as a foreign language based on a corpus containing 105 children’s written retellings of a short picture story: Written production in learner French ( https://spraakbanken.gu.se/en/resources/franska-elevtexter ). The children (aged 11 15) attended grades 6 (n=17), 7 (n=26), 8 (n=35), and 9 (n=27) in the Swedish school system. Because French is always studied after English in Sweden, it is considered a third language. The main aim of the studies was to investigate the role of previously acquired languages (Swedish and English) by examining lexical cross-linguistic influence. In written story retellings, some items are necessary to render such that a potential reader will understand its content, therefore detailed analyses of word choices have the potential to reveal cross-linguistic influence and the degree of lexical precision and accuracy. Overall, the results show that both Swedish and English have an impact on learners’ word choices, with English as the most important source for cross-linguistic influence. Word choices have also been examined from a vocabulary depth perspective by analyzing formal and morphological aspects. The results suggest that word part knowledge starts to develop in the early school years, but that spelling remains difficult throughout the four years. The corpus lends itself to many types of investigations of French learner language, such as the study of verb morphology, word order, and gender assignment, to name but a few.

t: Key issues in the development of a learner writing corpus to inform CEFR-aligned testing and assessment of school-age children
The distinction between the go-and-V and go-V sequences
Singular they Becoming even more Singular: The themselves/themself Variation on Reddit
abs: The pronoun they has seen increased attention and usage as a specific, sometimes non-binary-gendered, third-person pronoun in recent years. It has also begun to morphologically agree in number in the shape of the novel reflexive form themself . Social media users who declare their pronouns are the most plausible to use innovative pronoun forms and re-analyze the reflexive of they as number-sensitive based on their evident pronoun-awareness. In this study, I examine the use of themself by comparing such pronoun-declaring users on Reddit to two baselines, one composed of their peers in subreddit communities and the other being the general Reddit population. These Pronoun Declarers are represented with a novel corpus of 3M+ comments spanning from 2012 until 2021, with their counterparts sampled to ensure comparability in size and distribution. Samples are annotated and extrapolated to obtain estimates about the actual usage. Results indicate that themself usage has indeed increased in recent years, with the Pronoun Declarers and their peers using it more frequently than average. While their use patterns show expected sensitivity to number and specificity, it is still used less frequently than themselves for any antecedent, indicating that the potential change towards a number-sensitive reflexive of they is still emergent and sensitive to social conditioning. Still, this study may inform developers of language technology applications, authors of style guides, language educators, and anyone more generally concerned with inclusive language – themself is not a grammatical error but rather a novel and productive means to mark gender neutrality.

t: From ‘Thinking about’ to ‘Taking over’: Mapping the distribution and semantics of multiword verbs in L2 placement test essays
The language of GLP-1 medication in UK Media discourse: a diachronic perspective
abs: • The association between GLP-1 and type-2 diabetes management is in decline in UK news media. • GLP-1 news coverage is associated with a growing linkage with weight loss, lifestyle, body image, and the medicalisation of obesity. • GLP-1 news coverage resonates with discourses of individual responsibility and free will. • GLP-1s are commonly portrayed as a panacea for obesity, omitting references to public health interventions (e.g. promoting healthy diets and active lifestyles). This study examines the linguistic representation of GLP-1 analogues, a class of weight-loss medications originally prescribed for type 2 diabetes, in mainstream UK media texts. Using corpus methods (including frequency, collocation and concordance outputs), alongside discourse analysis, this study tracks and analyses emerging discourses surrounding GLP-1s and their evolution over time. This analysis covers articles published between 2006, when the first GLP-1 medication was approved in the UK, and 2025 (the present day at the time of writing). Findings indicate a declining association between GLP-1s and type 2 diabetes, and a growing linkage with weight loss, lifestyle, body image, and the medicalisation of obesity. These shifts in media representation reflect broader societal and medical changes, including evolving framing of obesity, notions of individual responsibility, and the positioning of GLP-1s within public health discourse. Such representations may influence patient expectations, treatment decisions and social attitudes towards diabetes and obesity. The study raises critical questions about the equity, accessibility and sustainability of GLP-1 treatments. It highlights the danger of portraying GLP-1s as a panacea for obesity, which may privilege the pharmaceutical industry over public health interventions such as promoting healthy diets and active lifestyles and may ultimately impact on public health literacy.

t: Task effects on the use of linguistic features in L1 and L2 production
Representing animals in ecological crises: A corpus-based ecological discourse analysis of 环球时报 (Global Times)
Lexical collocations in English as a Foreign Language (EFL) coursebooks: A corpus-based analysis of the usefulness score and pedagogical value
The grammar-lexicon trade-off in lexicography: Corpus-based categorization of STONE’s modifying uses
The Language of Hate and Offense: Understanding Linguistic Variation in Turkish Tweets
SCILIC and SCAWL: Developing a smart cities corpus and academic word list
abs: The rapid growth of smart city initiatives over the past two decades has led to a surge in research and practical applications. However, it has also resulted in significant terminological fragmentation across academic discourse, educational practices, and urban policy frameworks, posing challenges to achieving the educational and urban development targets outlined in the United Nations’ SDG 4: Quality Education and SDG 11: Sustainable Cities and Communities. To address this gap, the present study aims to develop and validate the Smart CIties LIterature Corpus (SCILIC) and to generate a word list from it through systematic corpus linguistic analysis. The corpus comprises 3.6 million tokens sourced from two primary domains: peer-reviewed articles indexed in Scopus and Web of Science (2015–2025) and technical reports from the UN-Habitat digital repository (2010–2025). Utilizing #LancsBox and complementary analytical tools, the study compiled a balanced and representative corpus and generated the Smart Cities Academic Word List (SCAWL), comprising 550-word families and 667 individual words. Quantitative analysis indicates that SCAWL accounts for 7.8% of the total corpus tokens. The findings underline the multidisciplinary nature of smart city vocabulary and highlight the importance of integrating both academic and policy-oriented sources. By supporting the development of targeted educational resources and promoting clearer conceptual understanding, this research contributes directly to the advancement of SDG 4 and SDG 11, fostering both educational quality and sustainable urban development.

t: Vocabulary in academic texts across disciplinary fields
abs: This article reports on a corpus-based study examining vocabulary of texts used as reading materials in two academic fields at a higher education institution in New Zealand: Computer Science (CS) and Media Design (MD). It first presents the vocabulary profiles of academic texts from both fields using Nation’s (2020) British National Corpus/Corpus of Contemporary American English (BNC/COCA) word frequency lists. Then, it outlines the vocabulary load required to comprehend different types of academic texts within the two corpora. The results indicate that while CS texts contain a wide range of mathematical, statistical, and programming-related lexical items, MD texts include a considerable number of proper nouns, such as the names of brands, companies, designers, and locations, as well as many non-English words. In terms of vocabulary demand, reading CS texts requires knowledge of 4,000 to 6,000 word families to reach 95% to 98% lexical coverage. In contrast, MD texts require knowledge of up to 8,000 word families for optimal comprehension across various text types. Interestingly, journal articles in both corpora show lower lexical demands than other types of texts, such as book chapters, textbooks, and materials sourced from online platforms (e.g., magazines, newspapers). The findings suggest that lexical demands vary when handling reading materials across different disciplinary areas in higher education, and provide insights into the extent of vocabulary knowledge needed to understand and learn different subject content through texts.

t: Linguistic stratification in academic publishing: A corpus-based analysis of lexicogrammatical variation across journal tiers
abs: • Journal tier correlates with distinct lexicogrammatical patterns in research texts • High-tier journals favor present-tense constructions and specific vocabulary • Low-tier journals prefer past-tense passives, generic verbs, and hedging • Linguistic stratification may create differential barriers for L2 scholars • Publication context systematically shapes acceptable academic discourse patterns This study examines linguistic stratification in academic publishing through corpus analysis of lexicogrammatical variation between high-tier and low-tier scientific journals. Using a specialized corpus of 2.3 million words from biochemistry, cell biology, and genetics publications, the research employs contrastive intralingual analysis to investigate how journal prestige influences language choices. Through key bundle analysis and examination of multiword units, the study reveals systematic differences in passive voice usage, tense selection, modal constructions, and lexical choices between journal tiers. High-tier journals demonstrate greater use of present tense constructions, specific vocabulary, and confident assertions, while low-tier journals show preference for past tense passives, generic verbs, and tentative modal expressions. The findings indicate that journal tier creates distinct linguistic expectations that reflect confidence versus tentativeness in academic writing. These patterns suggest that publication contexts systematically influence lexicogrammatical choices, with implications for how journal prestige shapes acceptable academic discourse and may create differential barriers for scholars navigating research publication in English.

t: Exploring engineering discourse through phrase-frames: Pedagogical recommendations
Speech and Language Disorders: A systematic review of corpora and future directions
abs: Speech and Language Disorders (SLDs) significantly impact social interaction, communication, and educational outcomes, making them a global health priority. According to data published by Komodo Health, speech disorder diagnoses among children aged 0–12 increased by 110% in 2022, reaching 1.2 million cases compared to the pre-pandemic average of 570,000. Addressing this growing challenge requires empowering the research community with diverse and comprehensive corpora to drive investigations and develop innovative tools. This paper systematically reviews existing SLD corpora, evaluating their relevance to research and technological innovation. The corpora are categorized based on target population, language, data modality, and task domain. Thirteen SLDs are explored, including neurological language breakdown, motor speech disorders, child language impairments, and communication challenges in autism spectrum disorder. The review identifies key research directions in the field of SLD and highlights critical gaps and challenges using statistical insights drawn from the analysed search. Emerging trends such as multimodal data integration and artificial intelligence applications for advanced data analysis are emphasised. The review concludes with recommendations for enhancing the utility and accessibility of SLD corpora, underscoring the importance of interdisciplinary collaboration and community engagement to address existing limitations. This review serves as a valuable resource for clinicians and researchers, guiding them in selecting the most suitable database/corpora to address their clinical and investigative needs while advancing the field of SLD research and innovation.
